title: Full-Stack Web Integration
blurb: Connect browser, backend, APIs, data flow, deployment, and architecture without repeating the dedicated Frontend course.

lessons.title: How browsers and servers communicate
objectives: Trace the full request/response cycle between browser and server
Explain how DNS changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DNS with HTTP request/response and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Typing a URL and hitting enter triggers: DNS resolves the domain to an IP, the browser opens a connection and sends an HTTP request, the server processes it and sends back an HTTP response (usually HTML/JSON/etc), and the browser renders or uses that response.
examples:
Browser --DNS lookup--> IP address
Browser --HTTP GET /--> Server
Server --HTTP 200 + HTML--> Browser
Browser renders the page
commonMistakes: Thinking of 'the frontend' and 'the backend' as unrelated systems rather than two ends of the same conversation.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the most commonly asked 'walk me through what happens when...' question in SWE interviews.

lessons.title: Frontend vs backend responsibilities
objectives: Draw a clear line between what belongs on each side
Explain how separation of concerns changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect separation of concerns with client-side vs server-side and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Frontend owns what the user sees and directly interacts with: layout, styling, client-side interactivity, and calling APIs. Backend owns business logic, data storage, security enforcement, and anything that must be trusted (never trust validation that only happens in the browser — the backend must re-check everything).
examples:
# Frontend: 'disable the submit button if the email field is empty' (UX nicety)
# Backend: 'reject the request if the email field is empty' (the REAL enforcement)
# Both matter -- but only one can be trusted.
commonMistakes: Relying only on frontend validation for anything that matters — a user can bypass your JavaScript entirely and hit your API directly.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing this boundary is exactly what separates junior full-stack work from senior.

lessons.title: The full-stack request lifecycle
objectives: Trace a realistic request end to end through a full-stack app
Explain how request lifecycle changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect request lifecycle with middleware and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A real request touches many layers in sequence: browser sends a request -> (optionally) a CDN/load balancer -> your backend server -> authentication check -> business logic -> database query -> response assembled -> sent back -> frontend updates the DOM with the result.
examples:
Browser -> Load Balancer -> API server -> Auth middleware -> Route handler
  -> Database query -> Response JSON -> Frontend renders it
commonMistakes: Debugging 'the app is broken' by guessing instead of tracing which layer actually failed (network tab, server logs, database) first.
lessons.careerRelevance: This layered debugging approach is exactly how real full-stack incidents get diagnosed on the job.
lessons.explain: A real request touches many layers in sequence: browser sends a request -> (optionally) a CDN/load balancer -> your backend server -> authentication check -> business logic -> database query -> response assembled -> sent back -> frontend updates the DOM with the result.

lessons.title: APIs and data flow between frontend and backend
objectives: Design a simple API contract that frontend and backend both agree on
Explain how API contract changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect API contract with JSON shape and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The API is the CONTRACT between frontend and backend: an agreed shape of requests and responses (usually JSON) that lets both sides be built and even changed somewhat independently, as long as the contract holds.
commonMistakes: Changing an API's response shape without telling the frontend team — a classic, entirely preventable full-stack breakage.
lessons.careerRelevance: API design is a shared skill both frontend and backend engineers are evaluated on in full-stack interviews.
lessons.explain: The API is the CONTRACT between frontend and backend: an agreed shape of requests and responses (usually JSON) that lets both sides be built and even changed somewhat independently, as long as the contract holds.

lessons.title: Deployment basics for a full-stack app
objectives: Explain, at a high level, how a full-stack app reaches real users
Explain how static hosting changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect static hosting with environment config and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A deployed full-stack app usually has: the frontend built into static files and served from a CDN or static host, the backend running as a containerized service behind a load balancer, and a managed database — all wired together with environment variables (API URLs, secrets) instead of hardcoded values.
examples:
# frontend: build -> static files -> CDN
# backend: Docker container -> cloud compute service
# both configured via env vars, e.g. API_BASE_URL, DATABASE_URL
commonMistakes: Hardcoding a 'localhost' API URL into the frontend build — it works perfectly until deployed, then breaks for every real user.
lessons.careerRelevance: This exact mistake is one of the most common first-deployment bugs new engineers hit.

lessons.title: Full-stack architecture, end to end
objectives: Describe a complete, coherent full-stack architecture for a real app
Explain how end-to-end architecture changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect end-to-end architecture with independent scaling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Putting it all together: a frontend (Frontend Development track) talks over HTTP to a backend (Backend Development track), which validates input, enforces auth, and reads/writes a database (Databases track); the whole thing is containerized (Docker) and deployed to the cloud (Cloud Computing) behind a load balancer.
commonMistakes: Treating frontend and backend as needing to scale together — in real systems they almost always scale independently, since their bottlenecks are completely different.
lessons.careerRelevance: This exact architecture is what most 'design a web application' system-design interview questions are really asking for.

exercises.title: Todo list (vanilla JS)

exercises.title: Fetch & render
exercises.prompt: Fetch JSON from a public API and render it into cards.

exercises.title: Trace the full cycle
exercises.prompt: Write out, step by step, everything that happens between typing a URL and seeing a rendered page.

exercises.title: Where does this validation belong
exercises.prompt: For 3 given rules (email format, password strength, unique username), say whether each belongs on the frontend, backend, or both — and why.

exercises.title: Design an API contract
exercises.prompt: Design the request/response shape for a 'create a comment' feature that both frontend and backend teams could build against independently.

exercises.title: Diagnose the layer
exercises.prompt: Given a bug report ('the page is blank'), list the 4 layers you'd check in order and what you'd look for at each.

exercises.title: Spot the deployment bug
exercises.prompt: A frontend works locally but fails in production with network errors. What's the most likely cause, and how do you fix it?

exercises.title: Sketch a full-stack architecture
exercises.prompt: Sketch (in words or a diagram) the full architecture for a simple blog: frontend, backend, database, and deployment, showing what scales independently.
